en: Now, the Gauḍapādīya-kārikās:
The all-pervading Viśva is indeed one whose consciousness is directed outward; Taijasa, however, is one whose consciousness is directed inward.
The one of dense wisdom and likewise the wise one are remembered as being just one, though existing in three ways. // 1.1 //
Viśva resides in the right eye, Taijasa within the mind, and Prājña in the space of the heart; thus he is established in three ways within the body. (1.2)
For Viśva always experiences gross objects, Taijasa experiences subtle objects, and Prājña experiences bliss; understand thus the threefold nature of experience. 1.3.
The gross [state] satisfies the Viśva, while the subtle [state] satisfies the Taijasa; likewise, bliss satisfies the Prājña—understand this threefold satisfaction. 1.4.
Whatever is proclaimed as the object of enjoyment and the enjoyer within the three abodes—he who knows both of these is not tainted while enjoying. 1.5
It is the settled conclusion that the vital breath (prāṇa) is the source of all existing beings; the vital breath generates everything, and the Puruṣa separately produces the rays of the mind. 1.6.
Others who contemplate creation consider it to be a manifestation or an emanation; by still others, creation is conceptualized as having the nature of a dream or an illusion. (1.7)
Those certain about creation hold that the Lord’s creation is by mere will;
those who contemplate time believe that the birth of beings proceeds from time. (1.8)
Some say creation is for the sake of enjoyment, others say it is for the sake of sport;
this is simply the nature of the Divine, for what desire can there be for one whose every wish is fulfilled? (1.9)
The Lord who brings about the cessation of all sufferings, the sovereign, the imperishable, non-dual with respect to all existents, is remembered as the fourth deity, the all-pervading one. (1.10)
The Viśva and Taijasa are held to be bound by both cause and effect;
the Prājña is bound by the cause alone; but these two do not apply to the Turya. (1.11)
The wise one perceives nothing at all— neither self nor others, neither truth nor even falsehood; that is the fourth state (*turya*).
He is the all-seeing at all times. // 1.12 //
The non-apprehension of duality is equal for both the Prājña and the Turya;
however, the Prājña is accompanied by the seed-sleep (bīja-nidrā), whereas that [sleep] does not exist in the Turya. (1.13)
The first two [states] are associated with dream and sleep; the *prājña* state, however, is characterized by the absence of both dream and sleep.
Those who are certain perceive neither sleep nor dream in the fourth state (*turya*).
For one who perceives otherwise, it is a dream; for one who does not know the reality, it is sleep.
When the error of these two is exhausted, one attains the fourth state.
When the individual soul, sleeping through beginningless illusion, awakens, it then realizes the unborn, sleepless, dreamless, non-dual reality. 1.16
If conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) existed, it would undoubtedly cease;
this duality is mere illusion (*māyāmātra*), for non-duality (*advaita*) is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). (1.17)
If the imagined were negated by someone, conceptual construction would cease; this teaching is for the sake of instruction, for when [reality] is known, duality does not exist. (1.18)
When there is no intention to express the universal (*viśva*), the universal of the initial [vowel] (*ādi-sāmānya*) is predominant;
and when there is no recognition of the measure (*mātrā*), it is precisely the universal of attainment (*āpti-sāmānya*) that occurs. (1.19)
In the cognition of the *taijasa* [subtle body], excellence is clearly observed; likewise, when there is no apprehension of the [gross] measures, there would be a state of duality. (1.20)
In the state of the syllable *m*, the wise man experiences the predominance of the commonality of mental activity (*mānasasāmānya*);
however, upon the attainment of the *mātrā*, there is indeed the commonality of dissolution (*layasāmānya*).
He who, being resolute, knows that which is equal and common in the three abodes— he is to be honored by all beings and is indeed a great sage worthy of reverence. 1.22.
The letter *A* leads to the Viśva state, the letter *U* likewise to the Taijasa, and the letter *M* further to the Prājña; beyond these, no further destination exists.
One should know the syllable *oṃ* part by part; the parts are the *mātrās*, without a doubt.
Having known the syllable *oṃ* part by part, one should not think of anything at all. (1.24)
One should yoke the mind to the *praṇava*; the *praṇava* is the fearless Brahman.
For one who is constantly disciplined in the *praṇava*, no fear exists anywhere. (1.25)
The syllable Om is indeed the lower Brahman, and the syllable Om is also remembered as the higher [Brahman].
The syllable Om is without prior, without interior, without exterior, without posterior, and is imperishable. 1.26.
For the *praṇava* is indeed the beginning of everything, as well as its middle and its end;
having thus known the *praṇava*, one attains that immediately thereafter. (1.27)
One should know the Praṇava as the Lord, residing in the heart of all;
having realized the Omkara as all-pervading, the wise man does not grieve. (1.28)
He by whom the syllable Om is known—that which is measureless, infinite in measure, the cessation of duality, and auspicious—is a sage, and no other person. (1.29)

[Colophon: Thus ends the first chapter, titled "Tradition" (*Āgama*), in the *Gauḍapādīya-āgama-śāstra*, which consists of the *Kārikās* of Gauḍapāda intended to reveal the meaning of the *Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad*.
Now begins the second chapter, titled "Unreality" (*Vaitathya*), in the *Kārikās* of Gauḍapāda.
The Second Chapter: The Chapter on Unreality (Vaitathya-prakaraṇa).
The wise declare that all things are unreal in a dream.
But because entities abide within [the mind], by reason of their being concealed. (2.1)
And because the time was not long, having traveled to those regions, he did not see them;
and upon waking, indeed, that entire place was no longer found.
And the non-existence of chariots and so forth is heard in accordance with reason; therefore, they say that unreality is indeed established as revealed in a dream. (2.3)
Because the distinctions exist within, it is therefore remembered that as it is there in the waking state,
so it is in the dream state, by virtue of being concealed.
The state of being concealed does not differ. // 2.4 //
For the wise say that the state of dreaming and the state of waking are one and the same.
For indeed, by means of the very reason well-known as the equality of the various distinctions. // 2.5 //
That which exists neither at the beginning nor at the end likewise exists not in the present;
though being similar to the false, they are perceived as if they were not false. (2.6)
Their purposiveness is contradicted even in a dream; therefore, because they possess a beginning and an end, they are indeed remembered as being false. (2.7)
For the qualities of those who dwell in heaven are indeed unprecedented and extraordinary.
Having gone there, he gazes upon them just as one who is well-trained would here on earth.

Even in the occurrence of a dream, that which is imagined internally by the mind is unreal, while that which is grasped by the mind as external is seen as real; thus, the falsity of these two is evident. (2.9)

Even during the waking state, that which is imagined internally by the mind is unreal, while that which is grasped externally by the mind is real; thus, the unreality of these two is established. (2.10)
If both states are equally unreal with respect to these distinctions, then who perceives these distinctions, and who indeed is their conceptualizer? (2.11)
The divine Self, by its own power of illusion (māyā), fashions itself as the self;
it is that very same [Self] which perceives the various distinctions—such is the certainty of the Vedānta. (2.12)
The Lord transforms other states of being situated within the mind— both those that are fixed and those that are unfixed— and likewise fashions those that are external to the mind. (2.13)
Those times which are internal to the mind, as well as those times which are external and consist of pairs—all these are merely imagined; their distinction is not caused by anything else. (2.14)
Those things which are indeed unmanifest internally, yet manifest externally, are all merely imagined; the distinction, however, lies in the different sense faculties.
First, the living being imagines a self, and thereafter various kinds of external and internal entities, according to its ignorance and according to its memory. (2.16)
Just as a rope that has not been ascertained is imagined in the dark through such entities as a snake or a stream of water, so too is the Self imagined. (2.17)

Just as when a rope is definitively ascertained, conceptual construction ceases and there remains only the non-duality of "it is just a rope," so too is the definitive ascertainment of the Self. (2.18)
It is conceptualized through these entities, beginning with the vital breaths and extending to the infinite.
This is the illusion of that god,
by which he himself has been deluded.

Those who know the vital breath call it "the breaths" (prāṇāḥ); those who know the elements call it "the beings" (bhūtāni); those who know the qualities call it "the qualities" (guṇāḥ); and those who know the principles call it "the principles" (tattvāni). // 2.20 //

Those who know the feet say they are the feet; those who know them as objects say they are the objects; those who know the worlds say they are the worlds; and those who know them as gods say they are the gods. (2.21)

Those who know the Vedas say, "The Vedas"; those who know the sacrifices say, "The sacrifices"; those who know the enjoyer say, "The enjoyer"; and those who know the object of enjoyment say, "The object of enjoyment. (2.22)
Those who know it as subtle call it subtle; those who know it as gross call it gross;
those who know it as embodied call it embodied; and those who know it as formless call it formless. (2.23)
Those who know time call it "time"; those who know the quarters call them "the quarters"; those who know arguments call them "arguments"; and those who know the worlds call them "the worlds. (2.24)

Those who know it as the mind call it *manas*; those who know it as the intellect call it *buddhi*; those who know it as the consciousness call it *citta*; and those who know it call it merit and demerit (*dharmādharma*). (2.25)
Some say there are twenty-five; others, twenty-six.
Some say there are thirty-one; and others, that they are infinite. (2.26)

Those who know the worlds say that the stages of life (āśramas) are the worlds; those who know that [truth] call them female, male, and neuter according to their gender-attributes (liṅga), while others call them the higher and the lower. 2.27.
Those who know creation call it "creation"; those who know dissolution call it "dissolution"; and those who know persistence call it "persistence"—yet here, all this is always everything. (2.28)
Whatever state a person shows to another, that very state the other perceives;
having become that [state], he protects it, and that grasping of it approaches him. (2.29)
By these non-distinct states, this [Self] is characterized as if it were distinct;
he who knows this according to reality may form conceptual constructions without hesitation. (2.30)
Just as dreams and illusions are seen, and just as a city of the Gandharvas is seen, so too is this entire universe seen by the wise in the Vedāntas. (2.31)
There is neither cessation nor arising, neither one bound nor a practitioner, neither one seeking liberation nor one liberated—this is the ultimate truth. (2.32)
This [world] is imagined through non-dual means by means of entities that are themselves non-existent;
and entities too are [imagined] by means of non-duality. Therefore, non-duality is auspicious. (2.33)

Those who know reality understand that this [world] does not exist through its own nature nor through the nature of another, nor in any way by itself; nothing whatsoever is either separate or non-separate. (2.34)
This non-conceptual state, the cessation of proliferation, which is non-dual, has indeed been perceived by sages who have transcended passion, fear, and anger, and who have mastered the Vedas. (2.35)

Therefore, having understood this, one should fix one's mindfulness upon non-duality; and having fully attained non-duality, one should conduct oneself among the world like an insentient being. (2.36)
Free from praise, free from salutation, and likewise free from the utterance of *svadhā*,
the ascetic, whose dwelling is both moving and unmoving, should live on whatever comes by chance.
Having seen the reality within and having seen the reality without, one becomes that reality; delighting in that reality, one shall not fall away from it. (2.38)
[Colophon: Thus [in the Gauḍapādīya-kārikā] / [B:
in the Gauḍapādīya Āgama-śāstra] / [S:
in the Gauḍapādīya-kārikās]]
The second chapter, titled "The Unreality" (*vaitathya*),
is concluded.
Now begins the third chapter, titled "Non-duality," from the Gauḍapādīya-kārikās. Oṃ.
Dharma based on ritual worship exists only after Brahman has been born;
prior to its birth, everything was unborn. Therefore, that [dharma] is considered pitiable. (3.1)
Therefore, I shall explain non-miserliness, which has attained the state of equality with the unborn, so that nothing whatsoever is born anywhere while being born. (3.2)
For the Self has arisen as individual souls like space, like the spaces within jars; and it has arisen through aggregates like the jars themselves—this is the illustration regarding birth. (3.3)

Just as when jars and other such objects have dissolved, the spaces within those jars and so forth merge completely into the [great] space, even so do the individual souls here merge into the Self. (3.4)

Just as when the space within one jar is joined with dust, smoke, and so forth, not all [spaces] are joined [with them], in the same way, the individual souls (jīvas) are [not all joined] with pleasure and the like. (3.5)
Indeed, in various places, names, functions, and forms differ;
yet there is no difference in space—such is the determination regarding the individual souls (jīvas). (3.6)
Just as the space within a jar is neither a modification nor a part of the [all-pervading] space, so too the living being (jīva) is never a modification nor a part of the Self (ātman). 3.7
Just as the sky appears stained with impurities to the ignorant, so too does the self appear stained with impurities to those lacking wisdom. 3.8
In death and in birth, and likewise in going and coming, he remains present within all bodies, like space— or rather, not like space.
Distinct in characteristic. // 3.9 //
All composite aggregates are like dreams, all of them projected by the self’s own illusory power; for no logical justification exists for either their superiority or their total equality. 3.10
For those sheaths beginning with "rasa," which have been explained in the Taittirīyaka,
their Self— the supreme living soul— has been clearly revealed as being like space. 3.11.
In each pair, within the knowledge of the honey, the supreme Brahman is revealed—just as space is revealed in both the earth and the belly. (3.12)
The non-difference between the individual self and the Supreme Self is praised through their identity, and that multiplicity which is censured is indeed consistent only in this way. (3.13)

That distinctness between the individual self and the Supreme Self which was proclaimed prior to creation is figurative, based on a future state of affairs; for actual primary distinctness is not possible. (3.14)
The various modes of creation taught through examples such as clay, iron, and sparks are merely means for instruction; there is no difference whatsoever [between the cause and its effects]. (3.15)
There are three types of spiritual stages (āśramas), characterized by inferior, middling, and superior views; this instruction on worship was taught for their sake out of compassion. (3.16)
Those who hold dualistic views remain firmly convinced of their own established tenets and contradict one another; yet this [non-dualist] is not contradicted by them. (3.17)
For non-duality is indeed the ultimate reality, while duality is said to be its differentiation;
since for them both types of duality exist, this [position] is not contradicted by that. (3.18)
For this unborn [reality] is divided only by illusion, and not otherwise in any way;
for if it were divided in reality, the immortal would fall into mortality. (3.19)
Proponents of [arising] desire the birth of an entity that is indeed unborn;
for how can an entity that is unborn and immortal come to mortality? (3.20)
The mortal does not become immortal, nor likewise does the immortal become mortal;
a transformation of intrinsic nature will never occur in any way whatsoever. (3.21)
If a thing that is immortal by its own nature undergoes mortality, how can that which is made immortal by artificial means remain stable? (3.22)
Whether a thing is created as real or as unreal, the scriptural statement remains the same;
that which is certain and endowed with reasoning is what is authoritative, and nothing else. (3.23)
From the Vedic revelation, "There is no diversity here," and also from "Indra by means of his powers of illusion," it follows that he,
though unborn, is born in many ways through illusion.
By the refutation of origination, arising is negated; by the question "Who indeed could produce this? the cause is negated. (3.25)
Since he denies everything explained as "not this, not this," he reveals the unborn through the reason that all things are ungraspable. (3.26)
For birth is possible through illusion, but not in reality; for one who is born in reality, that which was already born would have to be born again. (3.27)
The birth of that which is non-existent is not logically possible even through illusion; a barren woman’s son is born neither in reality nor even through illusion. (3.28)
Just as in a dream the mind vibrates through illusion with the appearance of duality, so too in the waking state the mind vibrates through illusion with the appearance of duality. (3.29)
The mind, though non-dual, appears as dual in a dream; of this there is no doubt.
Likewise, in the waking state, it is non-dual yet appears as dual; of this there is no doubt. (3.30)
This duality, consisting of whatever exists moving or unmoving, is the vision of the mind;
for when the mind becomes non-mind, duality is no longer perceived at all. (3.31)

When, through the realization of the truth of the self, one no longer forms conceptual constructions, then one attains the state of mindlessness; for when there is no object to be grasped, there is no grasping. (3.32)
They declare that non-conceptual, unborn knowledge is non-different from the object of knowledge;
the unborn, eternal Brahman, which is the object of knowledge, is realized by the unborn [knower] as being unborn. (3.33)
The movement of the wise one whose mind has been restrained and is free from conceptual construction should be understood as distinct from that of deep sleep; it is not the same. (3.34)
For that [mind] dissolves in deep sleep; when restrained, it does not dissolve.
That itself is the fearless Brahman, the light of knowledge extending in all directions. (3.35)
Unborn, sleepless, dreamless, nameless, formless, and ever-luminous—the omniscient one; there can be no metaphorical designation for him in any way whatsoever. (3.36)
Free from all verbal expression, arisen beyond all thought, perfectly tranquil, a single light, this samādhi is immovable and fearless. (3.37)
Therein is neither grasping nor relinquishing where no thought exists; then knowledge is established in itself, unborn and attained to equanimity. (3.38)
This so-called "yoga of non-contact" is difficult to perceive for all yogis; indeed, yogis fear it, seeing fear where there is no fear. (3.39)
For all yogis, freedom from fear, the destruction of suffering, awakening, and indeed imperishable peace depend upon the restraint of the mind. (3.40)
Just as the overflowing of the great ocean might be checked by a single drop with the tip of a blade of kusha grass, so too the restraint of the mind may be achieved through tireless effort. (3.41)
By means of skillful methods, one should restrain the mind when it is distracted by sensual enjoyments, and likewise when it is overly serene or in a state of lethargy; as is desire, so is lethargy.
Recalling that all is suffering, one should turn away from the enjoyments of the body of desire; recalling that all is unborn, one does not see anything born at all. (3.43)
One should awaken the mind when it is sluggish, and again pacify it when it is distracted;
one should recognize it when it is stained, and likewise recognize it when it is equanimous.
And one should not disturb what has been attained. // 3.44 //
One should not relish the pleasure therein; being free from attachment, one should become established through wisdom.
One should strive to unify the mind so that it is motionless and yet issues forth. (3.45)
When the mind neither dissolves nor is distracted again, being unwavering and free from appearances, then Brahman is realized. (3.46)
They describe the Omniscient One as self-abiding, peaceful, possessing nirvāṇa, ineffable, supreme bliss, unborn, and known by that which is unborn. (3.47)
No living being is ever born; its origination does not exist.
This is that supreme truth wherein nothing whatsoever is born. (3.48)
[Colophon: Thus ends the third chapter, titled "Non-duality" (*advaita*), in the *Gauḍapādīya-kārikā*, within the *Gauḍapādīya-āgama-śāstra*.]
Oṃ tat sat.
[B: The treatise is completed.
Now begins the fourth chapter, titled "The Quenching of the Firebrand":
He who, by means of knowledge resembling space, perceives phenomena as being like the sky...
I pay homage to that Perfectly Awakened One, the best among bipeds, who is non-different from the object of knowledge. 4.1
I bow to that which is called the yoga of non-contact, which brings happiness and benefit to all sentient beings, and which is taught as being free from dispute and contradiction. 4.2
For some proponents indeed maintain that what has come into being undergoes birth, while other wise ones maintain that what has not yet come into being does; thus they dispute with one another. (4.3)
Nothing that exists is born, nor does anything non-existent ever arise; thus, by disputing in this way, they proclaim non-arising as being dualistic. (4.4)
We approve of the non-arising (ajāti) proclaimed by them;
we do not dispute with them—understand this as being without contention. (4.5)
Proponents of [arising] desire the birth of a phenomenon that is indeed unborn;
for how can a phenomenon that is unborn and immortal undergo mortality? (4.6)
The mortal does not become immortal, nor likewise the immortal mortal;
a change of nature will never occur in any way whatsoever. (4.7)
If one's dharma, which is by nature immortal, falls into mortality, how can that which is made immortal by artificial means remain unshakable? (4.8)
That which is innate, natural (or "co-emergent"), and uncreated— that is to be known as *prakṛti*, which does not abandon its own nature. (4.9)
All phenomena are by their very nature free from aging and death; yet, those who desire aging and death fall away through that very mental conception. (4.10)
If an effect indeed has a cause, then that [cause] must itself be born as a cause.
How can that which is being born be unborn? And how can it be both distinct and eternal? (4.11)
If the cause is non-different from that [effect], then for you the effect would be unborn; for how could your cause be permanent if it arises from an effect that is being born? (4.12)
For one for whom there is the example of that which is born from the unborn, there is indeed no such thing;
and for that which is being born from what is already born, there is no established order (or rather, there is no lack of established order).
It follows as a logical consequence. // 4.13 //
For those for whom the cause has a beginning and the effect has a beginning, how can they describe the cause and the effect as being without beginning? (4.14)
For those for whom the cause is prior to the effect, and the effect is prior to the cause, their birth would be like the birth of a father from a son. (4.15)
If cause and effect are to arise, their sequence must be sought by you;
for if they were to arise simultaneously, there would be no connection between them, like [the two horns of] a cow. (4.16)
While it is arising from the fruit, your cause is not established;
how can a cause that is unestablished produce the fruit? (4.17)
If the establishment of the cause is from the effect, and the establishment of the effect is from the cause, which one is established first? [Which one arose previously?]
The accomplishment of which depends upon a relative reference.
"Either incapacity, or lack of full understanding, or else a violation of the proper sequence—thus, in every respect, have the Buddhas elucidated non-arising. (4.19)
The example known as the seed and the sprout is always equivalent to the probandum for us;
indeed, a reason that is equivalent to the probandum is not fit for establishing what is to be proven. (4.20)

The lack of knowledge regarding what precedes and what follows illuminates the fact that there is no birth; for how could that which is currently being born not be perceived prior [to its arising]? (4.21)
No entity whatsoever is produced either from itself or from another;
no entity whatsoever is produced that is existent, non-existent, or both existent and non-existent. (4.22)
Neither cause nor fruit arises by way of intrinsic nature, for they are beginningless.
For that which has no beginning, there is likewise no birth. (4.23)
The existence of the dependent nature is accepted because designation has a cause, otherwise there would be the destruction of duality, and because affliction is perceived. (4.24)
The fact that designation has a cause is accepted because of the observation of reasoning; the fact that the cause is itself without a cause is accepted because of the observation of reality. (4.25)
The mind does not touch the object, nor likewise the appearance of the object;
for since the object is unreal, the appearance of the object is not separate from it. (4.26)
The sign does not always contact the mind throughout the three times; how then can there be error for that which is signless? (4.27)
Therefore, the mind is not born, nor is that which is seen by the mind born; those who perceive its birth truly perceive a track in the sky. (4.28)
Since that which is unborn is born, therefore non-arising is its nature; there can never be any alteration of this nature. (4.29)
It will not be established that saṃsāra, which is beginningless, has an end;
nor will there be an infinity for liberation, which would possess a beginning. (4.30)
That which does not exist in the beginning and at the end likewise does not exist in the present;
though they are similar to what is false, they are perceived as if they were not false. (4.31)
Their purposiveness is subverted even in a dream, yet it is also affirmed; therefore, because they possess both a beginning and an end, they are indeed remembered as being purely false. // 4.32 //
All phenomena are false, as they are seen within the body in a dream; for how could there be a perception of elements in this enclosed space? (4.33)
It is not logical that [the soul] goes to see [the body], because there is no fixed time for such a journey;
moreover, once awakened, the entire [body] is not found in that location.
Having deliberated with friends and others, the awakened one does not proceed; and whatever has been grasped, once awakened, he no longer perceives. (4.35)
And in a dream, the body is without reality because it is seen as distinct from anything else;
as is the body, so too everything perceived by the mind is without reality. (4.36)
Because there is grasping, as in the waking state, that [grasping] is accepted as the cause in a dream;
and because it is the cause of that [grasping].
The waking state is held to belong to that very [self] alone. (4.37)
Since arising is not established, all things are declared to be unborn;
moreover, there can never be the emergence of a non-existent thing from an existent one. (4.38)
Having seen what is unreal while awake, one sees it in a dream, being absorbed in that;
and having seen even what is unreal in a dream, one does not see it upon waking. (4.39)
There is no non-existent thing that has a non-existent cause; likewise, there is no existent thing that has a non-existent cause.
There is no existent thing that lacks a real cause; how then could there be a non-existent thing that has a real cause? (4.40)

Just as one might, due to a cognitive distortion, perceive inconceivable things during the waking state as if they were real, so too does one see phenomena in that very same way within a dream due to a cognitive distortion. (4.41)

Because of perception and conventional practice, the Buddhas taught "birth" (jāti) to those who are always terrified of the unborn (ajāti), even though they assert the existence of real entities. (4.42)
For those who tremble at non-arising, because they perceive [things] as existing, the faults of arising will not be established; their fault, moreover, will be slight. (4.43)

Just as a "magical elephant" is spoken of because it is perceived and because of its conventional behavior, so too is a real entity said to exist because it is perceived and because of its conventional behavior. (4.44)

Manifesting as birth, manifesting as movement, and likewise manifesting as a real entity, consciousness is in truth unborn, motionless, and devoid of substantiality—it is quiescent and non-dual. (4.45)
In this way the mind is not born; in this way phenomena are known as unborn. Those who understand it exactly thus do not fall into error. (4.46)
Just as the flickering of a firebrand appears as straight, curved, and so forth,
so too does consciousness, through its own vibration, appear as the grasped and the grasper.
Consciousness is likewise a vibration. // 4.47 //
Just as a firebrand that does not move is without appearance, unborn, and unchanging,
so too consciousness that does not move is without appearance, unborn, and unchanging. 4.48
When a firebrand is moving, the appearances do not come from elsewhere; nor do they go anywhere else when it is motionless, nor do they enter back into the firebrand. (4.49)
They have not emerged from the firebrand because they lack the nature of a substantial entity;
the same would apply to consciousness as well, since there is no difference in the appearance.

When consciousness is indeed vibrating, appearances do not come from elsewhere; nor do they enter into that [consciousness] from elsewhere when it is motionless, for they are not distinct from it. (4.51)
They do not emerge from consciousness because they lack substantiality;
since they are always inconceivable, they possess neither the nature of cause nor effect. (4.52)

For one substance could indeed be the cause of another substance, and likewise one thing of another; however, neither substantiality nor the state of being something else is possible for [inhering] attributes (dharmas). (4.53)
Thus, phenomena are not born from the mind, nor is the mind born from phenomena; in this way, the wise enter into the non-arising of cause and effect. (4.54)
As long as there is the penetration of cause and effect, so long does the arising of cause and effect occur;
when the penetration of cause and effect has ceased, there is no arising of cause and effect. (4.55)
As long as there is the penetration of cause and effect, so long is saṃsāra extended;
when the penetration of cause and effect is exhausted, one does not enter into saṃsāra—saṃsāra no longer arises. (4.56)
Everything arises through conventional reality; therefore, there is indeed no eternalism.
For everything is unborn by way of its own-being; therefore, there is indeed no nihilism. 4.57
Those phenomena which are said to arise do not arise in reality;
their birth is like an illusion, and that illusion does not exist. (4.58)

Just as from a seed consisting of illusion an sprout consisting of that same illusion is born—neither of which is eternal nor subject to annihilation—so too is the application [of this principle] to all phenomena. (4.59)
In all phenomena, which are beyond the reach of speech, there is no designation of "eternal" or "non-eternal"; where letters do not operate, there "distinction" is not spoken of. (4.60)
Just as in a dream the mind moves with the appearance of duality through illusion, so too in the waking state the mind moves with the appearance of duality through illusion. (4.61)
The mind, though non-dual, appears as dual; of this there is no doubt in a dream.
The mind, though non-dual, appears as dual; of this there is no doubt in the waking state either. (4.62)
A dreamer moving about in a dream always sees living beings—whether born from eggs or born from sweat—who reside throughout the ten directions. (4.63)
Those objects perceived by the mind of the dreamer do not exist apart from it;
likewise, this very object of perception is held to be the mind of the dreamer itself. (4.64)
Wandering awake while one is awake, he constantly beholds those living beings— whether born from eggs or born from sweat— who reside within the ten directions.
Those objects are not found to exist apart from the waking consciousness that perceives them; likewise, this very visible world is held to be the mind of the waking state. (4.66)

For both of these are mutually visible; yet it is asked, "What is that which exists? According to that very [Buddhist] view, both are understood to be devoid of defining characteristics (lakṣaṇa). // 4.67 //
Just as a dream-like living being is born and also dies, so too all these living beings come into existence and cease to exist. (4.68)
Just as a life-spirit consisting of illusion is born and also dies, so too all these living beings come into being and cease to be. (4.69)
Just as an emanated being is born and also dies, so too all these living beings come into existence and cease to exist. (4.70)
No living being is born; its origination does not exist. This is that supreme truth wherein nothing whatsoever is born. (4.71)
This duality, appearing as the grasped and the grasper, is merely the vibration of the mind;
therefore, the mind is proclaimed to be eternally without object and unattached. (4.72)
That which exists by way of imagined convention does not exist in the ultimate sense;
[that which exists] by way of dependent convention is the dependent nature.
It may be that [it] does not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality. (4.73)
The unborn is so by way of imagined convention; in the ultimate sense, it is not even unborn.
By way of the dependent nature's manifestation, it is the dependent.
But it is born through conventional reality. // 4.74 //
There is an adherence to what is unreal; therein, duality does not exist.
Having realized the non-existence of duality, one becomes signless and is no longer born. (4.75)
When one does not find causes—whether superior, inferior, or middling—then the mind is not born; for in the absence of a cause, how can there be a fruit? (4.76)
The non-arising of the signless mind is equanimous non-duality, because all that is unborn is indeed the object of the mind's perception. (4.77)
Having realized the true state of signlessness and not obtaining any separate cause,
he then attains that fearless state which is free from sorrow and according to his desire.

For it is due to the adherence to what is unreal that [the mind] proceeds toward what appears similar; once it has realized the non-existence of the object, it turns back, free from attachment. (4.79)
For one who has desisted and does not engage [with objects], the state is indeed motionless; for that is the domain of the Buddhas—equanimity, unborn, and non-dual. (4.80)
Unborn, sleepless, and dreamless, it is itself the dawn; for this reality (dharma), by its very nature as the element (dhātu), is indeed once and for all illumined. (4.81)
"By the grasping of whatever dharma it may be, that Blessed One constantly conceals happiness and perpetually reveals suffering. (4.82)

"It exists," "it does not exist," "it both exists and does not exist," or again, "it neither exists nor does not exist"—the fool indeed obscures [reality] through these notions of movement, stability, both, or their absence. (4.83)
These four crores of grahas always surround him; he by whom the Blessed One is seen as untouched by these is all-seeing. (4.84)
Having attained complete omniscience, the state of brahminhood which is non-dual and devoid of beginning, middle, or end—what more could one possibly strive for beyond this? (4.85)
For this discipline of the wise is said to be tranquility in its primary sense; self-restraint arises from being naturally restrained. Knowing this, the learned man should attain tranquility. 4.86
That which possesses an object and involves apprehension is held to be mundane duality; that which lacks an object but involves apprehension is held to be pure mundane [knowledge]. (4.87)
Non-substantiality and non-apprehension are known as supramundane; this is the knowledge and the object of knowledge always proclaimed by the Buddhas. (4.88)
When the threefold knowledge and the object of knowledge have been understood in sequence by oneself, omniscience indeed arises everywhere for the one of great intelligence in this world. (4.89)
Those things to be abandoned, those to be known, those to be attained, and those to be matured should be understood according to their nature and their vehicle.
Apart from that which is to be known, perception regarding these three is traditionally taught. (4.90)
By their very nature, all phenomena are to be known as beginningless, like space;
for in them there exists no diversity whatsoever anywhere. (4.91)
All phenomena are by their very nature primordially enlightened and perfectly certain;
he who possesses such patient acceptance is fit for immortality. (4.92)
For all phenomena are primordially peaceful, unarisen, and by their very nature perfectly extinguished; they are all equal and undifferentiated—an unborn, equanimous, and fearless state. (4.93)
Indeed, there is no fearlessness for those who always dwell in division; prone to division and proponents of separate doctrines, they are therefore considered pitiable. (4.94)
But those who, in this present equality, shall become firmly resolved—they indeed possess great wisdom in the world, yet the world does not penetrate that [wisdom]. (4.95)
Knowledge is held to be unborn and non-transmigrating with respect to phenomena;
because knowledge does not proceed [into them], it is therefore proclaimed to be unattached. (4.96)
When even a minute difference arises, for one who is not wise, there is never non-attachment; how much less, then, could there be the falling away of obscurations? (4.97)
All phenomena are unobstructed and pure by nature;
they were enlightened from the beginning and thus liberated—so say the Leaders. (4.98)
For the wisdom of the Buddha does not proceed toward phenomena;
all phenomena are [all phenomena].
Likewise, this knowledge was not spoken by the Buddha. (4.99)
Having realized the state that is difficult to perceive, exceedingly profound, unborn, equanimous, confident, and free from multiplicity, we pay homage according to our strength. (4.100)
[Colophon: Thus ends the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad Kārikās composed by Gauḍapādācārya.
In the Āgama-Śāstra of Gauḍapāda, the fourth chapter, titled "The Quenching of the Firebrand," is completed.]
